top_comments.author: @AISA-AI
top_comments.text: The part most people miss with AI agents is that the skill isn't in setting them up, it's in knowing when to trust the output and when to intervene. An agent can run 50 steps autonomously but if you can't evaluate whether step 23 went sideways, you're just automating mistakes faster. The real skill with agents is designing good checkpoints and knowing what "done correctly" looks like before you hit run.

top_comments.author: @MarciLLyTV
top_comments.text: The part people underestimate most: agents don't just automate tasks, they change how you think about building workflows entirely. Once you stop designing for human-in-the-loop and start designing for agent-in-the-loop, your whole system architecture shifts. 2026 is the year most teams are going to feel that gap.

top_reply.author: @roslyngleave
top_reply.text: It's true, as it needs serious 'contraints' or 'guardrails' as it acts without explicit instruction. If you don't give it these - it could do things you don't want it to. You need to treat it a little like an employee you don't trust. Don't give it access to your e-mails, your bank details, your credit cards! Run it on it's own computer which is left on (so it can work all the time). It's not really for ai newbies. Start with VS Code, Claude Code or Codex or Claude Cowork :)
